inlines.text: There are infinitely many points on every line. Explain the use of the word

answer.short: There is no end to the number of points on a line.
answer.worked: However many points have been marked on a line, another point can always be chosen between two of them. Therefore no finite number counts all the points on the line.

inlines.text: There are infinitely many lines passing through every point. Explain the use of the word

answer.short: There is no end to the number of different lines that can pass through a point.
answer.worked: A line through a fixed point can have any direction. However many different lines have been drawn through the point, another direction can always be chosen, giving another line. Therefore no finite number counts all these lines.

content.prompt: There are four possible ways to place three distinct lines in a plane. Two of these configurations involve parallel lines, the other two do not. Draw all four of them, and find the one that encloses a region.

answer.short:
Three parallel lines; exactly two parallel lines crossed by a third; three non-parallel lines forming a triangle; three concurrent lines.

Only the triangular configuration encloses a region.
answer.worked:
With parallel lines, either all three are parallel, or exactly two are parallel and the third crosses both.

With no parallel lines, either the three lines intersect at three distinct points, enclosing a triangular region, or all three pass through one point and are concurrent.

These give the four configurations shown. Configuration 3 encloses a triangular region.

content.prompt: There are eight possible ways to place four distinct lines in a plane. Five of these configurations involve parallel lines; the other three do not. Draw all eight of them.

answer.short: The eight configurations are shown below: four parallel lines; three parallel lines and a transversal; two pairs of parallel lines; exactly one parallel pair with the other two lines meeting off both parallel lines; exactly one parallel pair with three lines concurrent; four concurrent lines; exactly three concurrent lines with no parallel pair; and no parallel pair or three concurrent lines.
answer.worked:
Classify first by parallel lines, then by concurrence.

With parallel lines there are five cases: all four parallel; three parallel and a fourth crossing them; two parallel pairs; one parallel pair with the other two lines meeting away from both parallel lines; and one parallel pair with the other two lines meeting on one of the parallel lines.

With no parallel lines there are three cases: all four concurrent; exactly three concurrent; and no three concurrent. The drawings illustrate these incidence relationships; rotations and changes of spacing do not create additional cases.

teachingContext.methodNote: A line extends infinitely in both directions. An interval includes both endpoints and all points between them. Both measured angles are $40^\circ$, so they are equal.

The four angles make one complete revolution about $L$.

$$\begin{aligned}5\alpha&=360^\circ\\\alpha&=72^\circ\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}2\alpha+\alpha&=90^\circ\\3\alpha&=90^\circ\\\alpha&=30^\circ\end{aligned}$$
(Adjacent angles forming right angle $BWX$.)

spec.description: Straight lines EG and NM with a downward ray to P. Retains theta, 60 degrees, gamma and 3 gamma; no printed vertex label or right-angle mark is added. Ordinary source blue becomes house black.

(Straight angle on $EG$.)
$$\begin{aligned}\gamma+3\gamma+60^\circ&=180^\circ\\4\gamma&=120^\circ\\\gamma&=30^\circ\end{aligned}$$

spec.description: One possible completed student construction, using a transversal at 45 degrees to the horizontal. J and K label its ends, and X and Y label its intersections with ST and UV.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Draw two vertical parallel lines, $ST$ and $UV$, using opposite edges of your ruler.

answer.worked: Draw along opposite edges of the ruler to obtain two vertical parallel lines. Label the left line $ST$, with $S$ above $T$, and the right line $UV$, with $U$ above $V$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Draw a transversal, $JK$, crossing these two parallel lines at an angle.

answer.worked: On the construction in part a, draw a sloping straight line crossing both parallel lines. Label points on its opposite ends $J$ and $K$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Let the transversal meet $ST$ at $X$ and $UV$ at $Y$.

answer.worked: Label the intersection of $JK$ and $ST$ as $X$, and the intersection of $JK$ and $UV$ as $Y$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Measure $\angle JXS$ and $\angle JYU$.

answer.short: Measurements depend on the construction; the two angles are equal. In the sample, $\angle JXS=135^\circ$ and $\angle JYU=135^\circ$.
answer.worked: Centre the protractor at $X$, align its baseline with $XJ$, and read the scale starting at $0^\circ$ on $XJ$. Repeat at $Y$ with the baseline along $YJ$. In the sample, $\angle JXS=135^\circ$ and $\angle JYU=135^\circ$.

children.label: e
children.prompt: Write down the result that these measurements confirm.

answer.short: If a transversal crosses two parallel lines, the corresponding angles are equal.
answer.worked: $\angle JXS$ and $\angle JYU$ occupy corresponding positions. Their equal measurements confirm that corresponding angles are equal when a transversal crosses parallel lines, here $ST\parallel UV$.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a transversal, measure two angles and identify the parallel-line relationship.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Draw two oblique parallel lines, $AB$ and $CD$, using opposite edges of your ruler.

answer.short: Two oblique parallel lines labelled $AB$ and $CD$.
answer.worked: Draw along one edge of the ruler and then its opposite edge without moving the ruler. Label the two parallel lines $AB$ and $CD$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Draw a transversal crossing these two parallel lines at an angle.

answer.short: A straight line crossing both parallel lines.
answer.worked: Add one straight line that intersects both $AB$ and $CD$, continuing the drawing in part a.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Let the transversal meet $AB$ at $X$ and $CD$ at $Y$. Label the endpoints so that $A$ and $C$ lie on the same side of the transversal.

answer.short: $X$ labels the intersection with $AB$; $Y$ labels the intersection with $CD$.
answer.worked: On the same drawing, label the intersection of the transversal and $AB$ as $X$, and its intersection with $CD$ as $Y$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Measure $\angle AXY$ and $\angle CYX$.

answer.short: Measurements depend on the drawing; the two measurements add to $180^\circ$.
answer.worked: Measure each angle with a protractor centred at its vertex and its baseline aligned with one arm, reading the scale that starts at $0^\circ$ on that arm. Since $A$ and $C$ lie on the same side of the transversal, $\angle AXY$ and $\angle CYX$ are co-interior angles. Their measurements add to $180^\circ$.

children.label: e
children.prompt: Write down the result that these measurements confirm.

answer.short: If a transversal crosses two parallel lines, the co-interior angles are supplementary.
answer.worked: $\angle AXY+\angle CYX=180^\circ$ (co-interior angles, $AB\parallel CD$). Thus co-interior angles formed by a transversal crossing parallel lines are supplementary.

classification.difficultyReason: Form converses and independently test the truth of each original statement and converse. No contrapositive is assessed.

content.prompt: State whether each statement below is true or false, then write down its converse. Then state whether the converse is true or false.

children.label: a
children.prompt: If you can run, then you can walk.

answer.short: True. Converse: If you can walk, then you can run. False.
answer.worked: The statement is true under the ordinary interpretation of these abilities. Reverse the condition and conclusion: If you can walk, then you can run. This converse is false: someone may be able to walk but unable to run.

children.label: b
children.prompt: If a number is greater than 10, then it is greater than 1000.

answer.short: False. Converse: If a number is greater than 1000, then it is greater than 10. True.
answer.worked: The statement is false: $20>10$, but $20<1000$. Reverse the condition and conclusion: If a number is greater than 1000, then it is greater than 10. This converse is true because $1000>10$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: If a man lives in Australia, then he lives in Melbourne.

answer.short: False. Converse: If a man lives in Melbourne, then he lives in Australia. True.
answer.worked: The statement is false: a man living in Sydney lives in Australia but does not live in Melbourne. Reverse the condition and conclusion: If a man lives in Melbourne, then he lives in Australia. This converse is true because Melbourne is in Australia.

children.label: d
children.prompt: If a number is divisible by 5, then its last digit is 5.

answer.short: False. Converse: If the last digit of a number is 5, then it is divisible by 5. True.
answer.worked: The statement is false: $10$ is divisible by $5$, but its last digit is $0$. Reverse the condition and conclusion: If the last digit of a number is 5, then it is divisible by 5. This converse is true by the divisibility rule for $5$.

children.label: e
children.prompt: If a woman has a daughter, then she is a mother.

answer.short: True. Converse: If a woman is a mother, then she has a daughter. False.
answer.worked: The statement is true because a woman with a daughter has a child. Reverse the condition and conclusion: If a woman is a mother, then she has a daughter. This converse is false: a mother may have only sons.

children.label: f
children.prompt: If a whole number has fewer than four digits, then it is less than 1000.

answer.short: True. Converse: If a whole number is less than 1000, then it has fewer than four digits. True.
answer.worked: The statement is true: a whole number with fewer than four digits is at most $999$. Reverse the condition and conclusion: If a whole number is less than 1000, then it has fewer than four digits. This converse is also true: the whole numbers from $0$ to $999$ have at most three digits.

children.label: g
children.prompt: If a dog has black and white hair, then it can stand on its hind legs.

answer.short: False. Converse: If a dog can stand on its hind legs, then it has black and white hair. False.
answer.worked: The statement is false: black and white hair does not guarantee that a dog can stand on its hind legs. Reverse the condition and conclusion: If a dog can stand on its hind legs, then it has black and white hair. This converse is false: a dog with another hair colour may be able to stand on its hind legs.

children.label: h
children.prompt: If one side of a rectangle has length $8\text{ cm}$, then its area is $40\text{ cm}^2$.

answer.short: False. Converse: If the area of a rectangle is $40\text{ cm}^2$, then one of its sides has length $8\text{ cm}$. False.
answer.worked: The statement is false: a rectangle measuring $8\text{ cm}$ by $2\text{ cm}$ has area $16\text{ cm}^2$. Reverse the condition and conclusion: If the area of a rectangle is $40\text{ cm}^2$, then one of its sides has length $8\text{ cm}$. This converse is false: a rectangle measuring $4\text{ cm}$ by $10\text{ cm}$ has area $40\text{ cm}^2$, but neither side has length $8\text{ cm}$.

content.prompt: Find the value of $\alpha$ in each diagram below.

spec.description: Two solid horizontal parallels and a red dashed auxiliary parallel, with matching rightward parallel marks. Two sloping segments meet at the central vertex. The 50-degree label denotes the whole angle between them.
spec.mathematics: The upper sloping segment makes 20 degrees with a horizontal parallel; the complete central angle is 50 degrees; alpha is the lower-right angle.
spec.answerVisibility: Only 20 degrees, 50 degrees and the unknown alpha are visible.

answer.worked:
The angle above the dashed line at the central vertex is $20^\circ$ (alternate angles, upper line parallel to dashed line). The angle below the dashed line equals $\alpha$ (alternate angles, lower line parallel to dashed line).
$$\begin{align*}\alpha+20^\circ&=50^\circ\quad\text{(adjacent angles)}\\\alpha&=30^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Right-angled triangle on a horizontal base extended right. The left side and the upper-right ray from the right base vertex carry matching parallel arrows.
spec.mathematics: Left base angle 55 degrees; top angle 90 degrees; unknown alpha at the right base. The additional ray is parallel to the left side.
spec.answerVisibility: The 55-degree given, right-angle square and alpha are visible; no derived angle is supplied.

answer.worked:
At the right base vertex, the angle between the extra ray and the rightward base extension is $55^\circ$ (corresponding angles, marked sloping lines parallel). The angle between the extra ray and the side leading to the top vertex is $90^\circ$ (co-interior angles, marked sloping lines parallel).
$$\begin{align*}\alpha+90^\circ+55^\circ&=180^\circ\quad\text{(straight angle)}\\\alpha&=35^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Two oblique transversals cross on the red dashed middle parallel, extending beyond the crossing to the left. Matching parallel arrows occur on all three horizontal lines.
spec.mathematics: The rising transversal makes 30 degrees with the top horizontal; the falling transversal makes 35 degrees with the bottom horizontal. Alpha denotes the complete left-hand angle at their crossing.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the two supplied numerical angles and alpha are visible.

answer.worked:
The two angles on the right of the crossing, above and below the dashed parallel, are $30^\circ$ and $35^\circ$ respectively (alternate angles, each outer horizontal parallel to the dashed line). Their sum equals $\alpha$ (vertically opposite angles).
$$\begin{align*}\alpha&=30^\circ+35^\circ\\\alpha&=65^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Upper and lower horizontal rays are parallel to a dashed red horizontal through the central vertex. A descending segment extends straight through the central vertex to the upper-left. Alpha lies between this extension and the segment rising to the upper ray.
spec.mathematics: The upper interior angle is 123 degrees and the lower interior angle is 150 degrees. Alpha is the exterior angle at the central vertex, not the angle between the two rightward sloping segments.
spec.answerVisibility: Only 123 degrees, 150 degrees and alpha are supplied.

content.prompt: There are five possible configurations of three distinct planes in space. Two involve parallel planes, and the other three do not. Draw a picture of each one.

answer.short:
The five configurations are:

1. Three parallel planes.
2. Two parallel planes cut by a third plane.
3. Three planes sharing one common line.
4. Three planes meeting pairwise in three distinct parallel lines, with no point common to all three.
5. Three planes with exactly one point common to all three.
answer.worked:
First consider parallel pairs. If every pair is parallel, draw three parallel planes. If exactly one pair is parallel, draw the third plane cutting both.

If no pair is parallel, every pair meets in a line. The three intersection lines can coincide, giving one common line; they can be distinct and parallel, giving no common point; or they can meet at one point, giving exactly one point common to all three planes. These are the remaining three configurations.

content.prompt: What is the angle between the minute and hour hand of an analogue clock at 12:15 p.m.? Hint: Why is it less than $90^\circ$?

answer.short:
$82.5^\circ$

The hour hand has moved $7.5^\circ$ past 12.
answer.worked:
The minute hand turns through $360^\circ$ in 60 minutes; the hour hand turns through $360^\circ$ in 12 hours.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Minute-hand turn}&=\frac{15}{60}\times360^\circ\\\text{Minute-hand turn}&=90^\circ\\\text{Hour-hand turn}&=\frac{15}{12\times60}\times360^\circ\\\text{Hour-hand turn}&=7.5^\circ\\\text{Angle between hands}&=90^\circ-7.5^\circ\\\text{Angle between hands}&=82.5^\circ\end{align*}$$

The angle is less than $90^\circ$ because the hour hand has moved towards 3.

content.prompt: How many minutes pass after 12 noon before the angle between the minute and hour hand is exactly $90^\circ$?

answer.short:
$16\frac{4}{11}$ minutes.

The minute hand gains $5.5^\circ$ on the hour hand each minute.
answer.worked:
The minute hand turns $360^\circ\div60=6^\circ$ per minute. The hour hand turns $360^\circ\div720=\frac12^\circ$ per minute.

Their separation first increases by $6^\circ-\frac12^\circ=\frac{11}{2}^\circ$ each minute. Let $t$ be the number of minutes after noon when they first form a right angle.

$$\begin{align*}\frac{11}{2}t&=90\\t&=90\times\frac{2}{11}\\t&=\frac{180}{11}\\t&=16\frac{4}{11}\end{align*}$$

The first right angle occurs $16\frac{4}{11}$ minutes after noon.

CHAPTER 6
Measurement and Geometry
An introduction to geometry
entries.exclusionReason: Chapter cover and subject identification; contains no practice task.

entries.description:
Geometry starts with some of the things that we see around us:
• the sharp line of the horizon out to sea
• the surfaces and edges of a city building
• the circular disc of the moon
• the path of a stone thrown through the air
• the wavy surface of the ocean
• the patterns on a cat’s fur coat
• the complicated patterns that clouds often make against the blue sky.

As in all of mathematics, we start with the very simplest patterns and gradually examine more complicated ones.

entries.description: The simplest objects of geometry are points, lines and planes. Because they are so simple, it is hard to give precise definitions of them, just as it is hard to say precisely what a number is. The following descriptions do not really say what points, lines and planes are, but they will help us to talk about them with some agreement about what they mean in our imagination.

entries.description:
Given two distinct lines in a plane, there are two possibilities:
• The two lines meet at a single point. This point is called the intersection of the two lines.
• The two lines have no point in common, no matter how far the lines are produced in either direction (the word ‘produced’ means ‘extended’). The lines are then called parallel lines.
The arrows on the two lines in the second diagram are used to indicate that the lines are parallel.

entries.description:

• There is exactly one line passing through two distinct points.
• Two distinct lines in the plane either meet at a point or are parallel.
• Two lines in a plane are called parallel if they never meet, no matter how far they are produced (meaning extended). This is written as AB ∥ PQ.
• Two lines parallel to a third line are parallel to each other.
• Three points that all lie on one line are called collinear.
• Three lines that all pass through one point are called concurrent.

The point A in the diagram to the right divides the line QAP into two pieces, called rays. The ray AP is the piece that contains the point P; it is drawn unbroken. The opposite ray, AQ, is the other piece of the line and contains the point Q.

Each ray includes the endpoint A, which is called the vertex of the ray. The two opposite rays AP and AQ have only the vertex A in common.

entries.description:
Angles
In the diagram on the left below, the two rays OA and OB have a common vertex, O.
We say that we have formed two angles. The first one is ‘between’ the two rays; the second is ‘outside’ the two rays.
We can describe the situations above using the idea of the amount of turning.
Imagine that the ray OA is rotated about the point O until it lies along OB. There are two ways of doing this:
[Figure 1] and [Figure 2]
The amount of turning in Figure 1 is smaller, and is called the size of the angle between OA and OB.
The amount of turning in Figure 2 is called the size of the reflex angle formed by OA and OB.
In this chapter, we will usually work with the smaller angle between two rays.

entries.description:
A revolution is the amount of turning required to rotate a ray about its endpoint until it falls back onto itself.

There are several systems of units for measuring the size of an angle. The best-known system divides the full revolution into 360 equal parts, called degrees, and was developed by Babylonian mathematicians in the ancient world. This system has an astronomical basis – there are about 365 ¼ days in the year, so the Sun moves approximately 1 degree (written as 1°) against the fixed stars every day.

The size of 1 revolution is 360 degrees, which is written as 360°.

Straight angle
A straight angle is the angle formed by taking a ray and its opposite ray. A straight angle is half of a revolution, and so has size equal to 180°.

entries.description:
Right angle
Let AOB be a line, and let OX be a ray making equal angles with the ray OA and the ray OB. Then the equal angles ∠AOX and ∠BOX are called right angles.
A right angle is half of a straight angle, and so is equal to 90°.
The conventional way to indicate a right angle is to use a small square at the vertex, as shown in the diagram to the right for ∠BOX.

entries.description:
A right angle is not an acute angle
A right angle is neither acute nor obtuse – it is the boundary between the two. Similarly, a straight angle is neither obtuse nor reflex, a revolution is not a reflex angle, and an angle of size 0° is not an acute angle.

entries.description:
Using a protractor to measure and construct angles
A protractor allows angles to be measured and constructed correct to about the nearest degree. The most common version consists of a semicircular piece of clear plastic with 181 equally spaced markers placed around its circumference, allowing the measurement of angles from 0° to 180°. Another type of protractor is a full circle with 360 equally spaced markers, allowing the measurement of angles from 0° to 360°.

The steps for measuring or constructing an angle are almost the same.

entries.description:
• A revolution is 360°, a straight angle is 180° and a right angle is 90°.
• An acute angle has a size between 0° and 90°.
• An obtuse angle has a size between 90° and 180°.
• A reflex angle has a size between 180° and 360°.
• The size of an angle is normally taken to be between 0° and 180°.
• When the reflex angle is required, it is written as ‘reflex ∠AOB’. The reflex size of an angle is between 180° and 360°. Notation such as ∠AOB normally refers to the angle between 0° and 180°.
• Two angles are called complementary if they add to 90°.
• Two angles are called supplementary if they add to 180°.
• Angles can be approximately measured and constructed with a protractor.

entries.description:
Angles at a point – geometric arguments

Clear, logical reasoning has always been an important part of geometry. Diagrams make it easier to understand and construct convincing arguments in geometry and in many other branches of mathematics.

When setting out geometric arguments, we state the appropriate reason in brackets after any geometric statement. Reasons should always be as specific as possible and should name any figure that they refer to.

This section develops four reasons that can be given when dealing with problems about angles at a point.

entries.description:
When two lines intersect, four angles are formed at the point of intersection. The two marked angles ∠AOX and ∠BOY are called vertically opposite angles, because they are opposite each other across the vertex O.
These two angles are always equal. To see this, note that:
∠AOX + ∠BOX = 180°
∠BOY + ∠BOX = 180°
therefore: ∠AOX = ∠BOY

entries.sourceLabel: Using Greek letters for angle size
entries.description:
Letters are very useful in geometry, as in all mathematics. In this book, angle sizes will usually be represented by lower-case Greek letters. Four Greek letters will be sufficient at this stage:
• α, called alpha (the Greek letter a)
• β, called beta (the Greek letter b)
• γ, called gamma (the Greek letter g)
• θ, called theta (the Greek letter for th).
The English word alphabet comes from the first two letters of the Greek alphabet – alpha and beta.

entries.description:
Perpendicular lines
Two lines are called perpendicular if they intersect so that the four angles formed are right angles.
Because adjacent angles on a straight line are supplementary, and vertically opposite angles are equal, it is only ever necessary to prove that one of the four angles is a right angle.

entries.description:
Angles at a point – geometric arguments
• Four reasons to be used in arguments (preferably with the names of vertices):
1 Adjacent angles can be added and subtracted.
2 Angles in a revolution add to 360°.
3 Angles in a straight angle add to 180°.
4 Vertically opposite angles are equal.
• Two lines are called perpendicular if they meet at right angles.
• Four Greek letters – α (alpha), β (beta), γ (gamma), θ (theta) – are often used to represent angle sizes in geometry.

entries.description:
Suppose now that the two lines are parallel, as in the diagram shown. In this situation, the co-interior angles ∠AFG and ∠CGF, marked α and β, cannot be equal, because one is acute and the other obtuse (unless they are both right angles).
The co-interior angles are supplementary; that is, their sum is 180°.
To prove this, we note that:
∠BFG = β (alternate angles, AB ∥ CD).
Hence, α + β = 180° (straight angle at F).
When you use this result, you will need to mention co-interior angles and name the parallel lines, as in the next example.

entries.description:
In the diagram to the right, the two alternate angles ∠BFG and ∠FGC, both marked θ, are equal.

Hence, ∠DGX = θ (vertically opposite at G).

Therefore, the lines CD and AB are parallel.

When using equal alternate angles to prove that two lines are parallel, the reason must be stated as ‘alternate angles are equal’, as in the next example.

entries.description:
Proving that two lines are parallel
Suppose that a transversal crosses two other lines.
• If the corresponding angles are equal, then the lines are parallel.
• If the alternate angles are equal, then the lines are parallel.
• If the co-interior angles are supplementary, then the lines are parallel.

entries.description:
A statement and its converse
The statements in this section are the converses of the statements in Section 6E, meaning that they are formed from the previous statements by reversing the logic. For example:
Statement: If the lines are parallel, then the corresponding angles are equal.
Converse: If the corresponding angles are equal, then the lines are parallel.
Pairs such as these, consisting of a statement and its converse, occur routinely throughout mathematics, and are particularly prominent in geometry. In this case, both the statement and its converse are true.
It is most important to realise that, in general, a statement and its converse are quite different. Never assume that because a statement is true, then the converse must be true. For example, consider the following statement and its converse.
Statement: If a number is a multiple of 4, then it is even.
Converse: If a number is even, then it is a multiple of 4.
The first statement is clearly true, but its converse is false, because, for example, 10 is even but is not a multiple of 4.
Here is an example from surfing.
Statement: If you catch a wave, then you will be happy.
Converse: If you are happy, then you will catch a wave.
Many people would agree with the first statement, but everyone knows that its converse is plain silly – you need skill to catch waves, not happiness.
Thus, the truth of a statement has little to do with the truth of its converse. Just as much care has been taken in justifying the converse statements in this section as was taken in justifying the original statements of the previous section.

entries.description: Find the size of ∠AOB in diagram a.

O lies on a horizontal straight line with B on the right-hand ray. Two further rays extend upper-left and upper-right; A labels the upper-right ray. entries.description: Find the size of ∠AOB in diagram c.

entries.presentation: Preserve the adjacent angle sectors and A, B, O labels.

entries.presentation: Review exercise; PDF page 42, printed page 184. Four parts in source order a, b, c, d, arranged in two columns.

entries.description: Find the value of α in diagram a.

Two horizontal blue lines and a red dashed horizontal line between them have matching parallel arrows. A zigzag joins the upper-right endpoint through a central leftward vertex on the dashed line to the lower-right endpoint. The upper-right interior angle is 20°, the full angle between the two sloping segments at the central vertex is 50°, and the lower-right interior angle is α.
entries.presentation: Keep the dashed parallel scaffold and all parallel markings; 50° spans both sloping segments.

entries.description: Find the value of α in diagram b.

A triangle has a horizontal base extended to the right. Its left base angle is 55°, its top vertex has a right-angle square, and its right base interior angle is α. A ray extends upper-right from the right base vertex and carries the same parallel arrow marking as the triangle's left side.
entries.presentation: Preserve the right-angle marker, base extension and marked parallel pair.

entries.description: Find the value of α in diagram c.

Two blue horizontal lines and a red dashed horizontal line between them carry matching parallel arrows. Two sloping lines cross on the dashed line. One reaches the upper-right horizontal endpoint, making 30° there; the other reaches the lower-right horizontal endpoint, making 35° there. Both extend beyond the intersection to the left. α labels the left-hand angle between the two sloping lines.
entries.presentation: Preserve both transversal extensions, the dashed parallel scaffold and the position of α.

entries.description: Find the value of α in diagram d.

Upper and lower blue horizontal rays point right, with a red dashed horizontal line between them; all have matching parallel arrows. From a central vertex on the dashed line, one segment rises right to the upper horizontal ray, where the interior angle is 123°. Another descends right to the lower horizontal ray, where the interior angle is 150°, and extends through the central vertex towards the upper-left. α is between that upper-left extension and the segment rising right.
entries.presentation: Preserve the straight extension through the central vertex and the exterior position of α.
